concepts.title: Art as the Human Need to Express
concepts.definition: Art answers a basic human need to express -- feelings, faith and experience communicated to others through form. From prehistoric rock paintings onward, Indians expressed through art, and the performing arts -- music, dance, drama -- carry that expression through time, gesture and sound.
concepts.key_idea: Expression is a basic need; the performing arts are its oldest public voice.
concepts.textbook_ref: keks103.txt opening (arts important in human life, expression communicated through arts, prehistoric expression, diversity of art forms)

solution_steps.explain: Human beings must express; art is the shaped form that expression takes.
Prehistoric evidence shows expression through art long before writing -- art precedes letters.
Music, dance and drama perform expression live, binding performers and audience in one event.

concepts.title: Music, Dance and Drama as Traditions
concepts.definition: India's performing arts grew as traditions with rules and lineages: classical music in its systems of melody and rhythm, dance forms that weave gesture and story, and drama blending speech, song and action. Folk and regional forms ran alongside, so the tradition lives in many voices.
concepts.key_idea: Tradition means trained continuity -- ragas, repertoires and gesture languages handed down while folk forms keep it rooted.
concepts.textbook_ref: keks103.txt tradition sections (music systems, dance forms, drama, folk traditions, guru shishya parampara, classical and regional forms)

solution_steps.explain: Music organised melody and rhythm into systems; dance codified gesture and expression; drama united both with word.
The guru-shishya path handed living skill from teacher to student, keeping traditions exact and alive.
Regional and folk forms carried the same expressive need in local idioms -- the tradition's widest layer.

concepts.title: Performing Arts as Cultural Memory
concepts.definition: Beyond entertainment, the performing arts store cultural memory: epics, devotional currents and social values travel through songs, dances and plays. Patronage by temples, courts and communities kept the arts central to festivals and rites, making performance a living archive of the civilisation.
concepts.key_idea: Stage and courtyard are archives -- epics and values survive because they are performed, not only written.
concepts.textbook_ref: keks103.txt memory sections (epics in performance, devotional music, patronage, festivals, arts as living heritage)

solution_steps.explain: Themes from epic and devotion, encoded in ragas and choreographies, carry history in the body.
Temples, courts and village communities funded and staged the arts, embedding them in social life.
Each festival performance re-reads the tradition for a new audience -- memory renewed, not merely kept.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Explain why the guru-shishya method, rather than books alone, kept the performing arts alive for centuries.

solution_template.explain: Music and dance live in the body and ear, not on paper -- subtleties resist notation.
Long study beside a guru transmits exact practice, correction and taste person to person.
Embodied art needs embodied teaching -- which is why the parampara outlasts centuries.

worked_examples.question_pattern: A village festival stages an episode from the Ramayana as folk theatre. Show how this performance works as cultural memory.

solution_template.explain: The epic story, its values of duty and devotion, ride inside the performance.
Each year's staging re-tells the episode for a new audience, including children.
The village has archived and re-transmitted its heritage without a single page -- performance as memory.
